record.paper_title: RELATIVISTIC JETS: OPEN PROBLEMS AND CHALLENGES
record.original_question: If long/soft gamma-ray-burst jets are accelerated magnetically and later undergo rarefaction acceleration after leaving the progenitor star, how can that scenario explain reports of very early jet breaks in afterglow light curves, and do such very early jet breaks actually occur in real bursts?

evidence.quote: It is unclear how this scenario could accommodate very early jet breaks, although further observations are needed to verify that such breaks really exist.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a model of long/soft gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) in which the relativistic jet produced by the central engine is accelerated primarily by magnetic forces while it is collimated inside the progenitor star, and then experiences an additional sudden boost in Lorentz factor via a magnetosonic rarefaction wave at the moment it breaks out of the stellar envelope into a much lower-pressure environment (rarefaction acceleration). Under this scenario, the post-breakout jet has a relatively wide opening angle and a moderate-to-high terminal Lorentz factor, which generically predicts a panchromatic afterglow jet break on time-scales of order one day or later.

(a) Within this magnetic + rarefaction-acceleration framework, determine whether it is possible to produce a panchromatic jet break in the afterglow light curve at very early times (of order one hour or less after the burst), corresponding to inferred jet half-opening angles of less than about one degree, and if so identify the physical conditions (e.g., magnetization, geometry of the progenitor cavity, ambient density, energy distribution with angle) that would be required.

(b) Determine, on the basis of GRB afterglow observations, whether such very early jet breaks (on hour time-scales) genuinely occur in real bursts, or whether the features previously interpreted as such breaks admit alternative explanations (e.g., energy injection, structured jets, viewing-angle effects, or transitions in the external medium).
artifact.status_search_result: The tension between magnetic/rarefaction-acceleration scenarios (which favor jet breaks at ≳1 day) and reports of hour-scale early jet breaks remains unresolved. Subsequent MHD studies (Komissarov et al. 2010; Granot et al. 2011) confirmed that rarefaction acceleration naturally produces late breaks, while observational identification of genuine very-early jet breaks is still ambiguous, with recent works (e.g., on the BOAT GRB 221009A) showing breaks may even be absent. No definitive resolution has appeared.

status_evidence.title: Rarefaction acceleration of ultrarelativistic magnetized jets in gamma-ray burst sources
status_evidence.snippet: Afterglow light curves of GRB outflows accelerated through efficient magnetic-to-kinetic energy conversion would either exhibit a very early jet break or show no jet break at all.
status_evidence.claim: Magnetic-acceleration scenarios predict either very early or no jet break, motivating the rarefaction-acceleration refinement.

status_evidence.title: Rarefaction acceleration in magnetized gamma-ray burst jets
status_evidence.snippet: The rarefaction-acceleration mechanism can give rise to magnetically accelerated outflows allowing a late panchromatic jet break on time-scales greater than 1 day.
status_evidence.claim: Rarefaction acceleration predicts late (≳1 day) jet breaks, leaving very early breaks unexplained within this framework.

status_evidence.title: TeV Afterglow of BOAT GRB without Jet Break
status_evidence.snippet: TeV Afterglow of BOAT GRB without Jet Break
status_evidence.claim: Recent observations show that even very energetic GRBs may lack a clear jet break, indicating the question of jet-break timing remains observationally open.
